title: Bendōwa 4 - Zen Practice as Expressing Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk is that enlightenment is not something separate from practice, but rather it's the natural state of being that can be accessed through zazen (meditation). Rather than striving to achieve enlightenment, we should simply sit in the present moment and allow ourselves to be, as Uchiyama Roshi emphasizes. This understanding offers a profound yet unassuming perspective on enlightenment, one that values harmony, quietness, and effortless realization over forced effort or struggle.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Sorry I wasn't here last week.
I hope Andrea gave an interesting talk.
I'm sure she did.
I was leading a retreat on self-compassion in Tacoma, in both places.
Actually not in Tacoma, but on the water nearby.
I had a former convent, now turned into a retreat center.
And yeah, I got the big promotion that I'm not here.
I'm sure next week I'm in Costa Rica, so I'll just drop in from time to time, see how it's going.
The next two weeks, week and a half, I'll be in Costa Rica.
Just me and Janet.
And the birds.
We have like 460 species of birds in our vast country.
Costa Rica, which is like the size of Whatcom County or something like that, not too much bigger, has 860 or something like that.
Very diverse.
So I'll bring back a report in Costa Rica.
According to the main biography of Dogen, let's continue considering Dogen in his early essay, Bendowa, on the endeavor in the way.

According to the main biography about him, which is the source of many of the stories about what his life was like and what happened with him, and which was actually written 200 years after he died, he had a burning question.
Dogen had a burning question in his life and in his practice that inspired him to look beyond his initial training in Tendai Buddhism and beyond Buddhism in Japan altogether.
He's quoted as saying this to himself.
Who knows 200 years later if he really said this to himself, but he might have.
He said:
*As I study both the exoteric and esoteric schools of Buddhism, they maintain that human beings are endowed with Dharma nature by birth.
If this is the case, why did the Buddhas of all ages, undoubtedly in possession of enlightenment, find it necessary to seek enlightenment by engaging in spiritual practice?*
In other words, he'd been taught by his teachers and by the tradition that we're already awake, we're already okay, we have this Buddha nature.
Our nature is to be luminous and open and alive and be okay.
So why do we need to practice?
According to the stories, his teachers never had a very good answer to that.

He felt like he got a little better answer when he transferred from the mountain monasteries on Mount Hiei to the temple of [unclear: "Kinnunji"], which had a Zen influence but wasn't quite a Zen temple yet.
And then he went off to China.
But it's interesting to think about, what's your question?
Do you have a question about your life?
Maybe that question doesn't show up in words.
I remember early in my practice, one of the teachers where I was, he was big on this idea of having a question.
So periodically during the practice period he'd invite everybody to come to Dokusan and tell him what your question is.
I'd be so embarrassed, I didn't have a good question.
My question, I guess, is I don't know what my question is.
So that's a good question.
So Dogen had this question, supposedly.
And the conclusion he came to, assuming that was his question, is pretty subtle, in the sense that it's hard for our usual discursive thinking minds to hold his answer.
Our discursive mind is like, it's either this or it's that, it's better, it's worse, it's good for me, it's bad for me, right?
This answer doesn't really fit in those kinds of categories.
To me, Dogen's answer is more like a feeling for our life, and you can't quite explain it.
I'm always wishing that I could rest more fully in this feeling that Dogen offered to us, passed down to us, in a way, through Suzuki Roshi and Norman and everybody in between.
There's a Japanese teacher, Uchiyama Roshi, who was part of a little zazen reform movement in the late 19th and early 20th century in Japan.
He ended up having some important American and Japanese students who recorded his talks and wrote them down.
So there's a book of commentary called The Whole-Hearted Way, which is Uchiyama Roshi commenting on this text of Dogen, Bendowa.

And the Dogen piece we're going to study this weekend at the study seminar, his instructions to the cook, there's also a book about Uchiyama's commentary on that, called Cooking Your Life or something like that.
Anyway, here's what Uchiyama Roshi said, at least as they translated it:
*Dogen Zenji said that to sit in such a way is the true way of enlightenment.
To sit in just such a way is the true way of enlightenment.
That zazen itself is enlightenment.
Zazen is not a means to gradually attain enlightenment.
We sit zazen, which is dropping off body and mind right now, right here.
Practice and enlightenment are not something different.
We should not separate practice and enlightenment into two.
Since zazen is itself enlightenment, there is no way to think that I become enlightened as a result of zazen practice.
To sit zazen is to be in the profound sleep of enlightenment.*
Turn that over in your mind for a minute.
To sit zazen is to be in the profound sleep of enlightenment.
So if you're a little sleepy sometimes during zazen, this is good.
We're dreaming enlightenment.
He goes on:
*Therefore to think that I am enlightened is the same as to think that I sleep well within sound sleep.
But this is actually sham sleep.*
These guys are always that way.
Oh, you think it's this way?
Oh, no, it's not that way.
It's another way.
*When we sleep really well, we cannot think that we sleep well.*
How could you?
When you're sleeping well, you don't think, oh, this is good, I'm sleeping well.
You're just sleeping.
*In the same way within zazen we cannot see if we're enlightened or not.
Sometimes we feel clear in zazen, sometimes not.
Certainly we don't feel clear more often than not.*
This is a very experienced meditator.
*We don't feel clear more often than not.
But in either condition it's okay.
Zazen is zazen.
We sit right in that place where we can look at both enlightenment and illusion equally.*
Like so many things in Buddhism, it can be easier to talk about what it's not.
So zazen practice, he's saying, is not about fixing us.
It's not like we're not enlightened now and we'll be enlightened later.
Like we're broken and we need some repairs.
And yet it's not like there's no enlightenment either.
It's just that it can't be grasped onto in that way.
It can't be made into an object that we can manipulate and get or hold or use.
So this is the [unclear: "zan"] of Dogen and Suzuki Roshi and Norman too, I suppose.
There are many different Buddhisms and many different [unclear: "zans"].
And probably it is useful to have this concept of awakening or enlightenment.
It's probably a useful idea.
It's more like a lodestar, like a north star.
The north star helps us know which direction we're going, right?
But we never have the idea, one day if I just walk long enough I'm going to reach the north star.
We don't have that idea.
So maybe enlightenment is a little bit more like the north star.
It helps us have direction in our life.
But some people see enlightenment as much more directly a particular experience, an important experience you can have.
And there's nothing wrong with that either.
This debate has been going on forever, thousands of years.
Sometimes they call it the debate between sudden and gradual enlightenment, which is a little simplistic, but more or less we're a gradual school.
If you haven't figured that out yet.
Very gradual.
So gradually you can't tell that there's anything graduating there.
But the other school was wonderful too.
And this debate goes on, just the other day on Facebook.
The debate continued.
A teacher I know and like named James Ford posted a provocative article saying, big mistake to let enlightenment drop out of Zen.
Zen is all about awakening.
So you fools that are dropping it out, that's really bad.
Here's a little part of his article:
*In the Western Zen scene today, words like enlightenment, Kensho and Satori have been pushed to the background.
Any emphasis on the experience of awakening has been minimized.
There are reasons for this and I think some of them are legitimate.
However, that acknowledged, the great project of Zen is nothing less than awakening.
And sliding over that and shifting the point to something else is making a terrible mistake.*
Terrible mistake, he says.
And of course I couldn't help it.
I joined the conversation with several of my colleagues.
It's not like we're ever going to figure anything out on Facebook, whether it's politics or enlightenment, but still we have to try.
It was mostly pretty respectful.
But later I got a private message from another Zen teacher saying, I saw that thing you posted on there and I think you just didn't get it.
You didn't get what James was trying to say there.
I'm like, okay, thank you for telling me.
But I also agreed, of course, with what James was saying.
The project of Zen is the project of awakening.
But the devil's in the details.
And in the spirit.
And love is in the spirit too.
So let's go back to Dogen himself.
How does Dogen try to express this?
I was trying to make sense of the last four or five paragraphs, which bend over and through themselves and repeat themselves a lot.
So what I decided to do was pick out a few different expressions from the last several paragraphs of Bendowa and read you what Dogen wrote and comment a little bit.
So this is not even in order and it's excerpted.
It's not the whole thing that he wrote.
Dogen wrote:
*The mind of the person seated in Zazen and the [unclear: "enlightenment"] all around enter realization and leave realization within the stillness of Samadhi as it occurs within Jijuyu Samadhi.
And this does not disturb a single mode of dust.
The mind of the person seated in Zazen and the environment all around enter realization and leave realization within stillness, within the stillness of Samadhi, within the sphere of Jijuyu Samadhi.*
Remember that self, the enlightenment that takes care of itself, the joyful enlightenment that takes care of itself, is Dogen's enlightenment.
So we don't have to make it happen.
It takes care of itself.
But the beautiful thing in this expression, I think, is this sense of no resistance.
We move into realization, out of realization, and nothing's disturbed, not even the dust.
We're so graceful and we're so relaxed about it.
It's not a big problem for us if one moment we feel more deluded and another moment we feel more enlightened.
And there's a powerful sense of harmony.
That this is profound and important, but it's also not a big deal.
Whatever this realization, awakening, enlightenment is, it's quiet.
